readings.title: Heidi: the climb from Mayenfeld (Chapter I, first part)
readings.challenge: Build a picture of a character from what other people say before he ever appears.
readings.focus: Village talk makes the Alm-Uncle frightening long before the reader meets him.
readings.context: Heidi (1880–81) is by the Swiss writer Johanna Spyri; this English translation by Elisabeth P. Stork appeared in 1915. Deta, a young woman of twenty-six, is taking her five-year-old niece Heidi up a mountain in Switzerland. An Alm is a high mountain pasture; Mayenfeld, Doerfli and Praetiggan are places in the Swiss Alps, and Frankfurt is a large city in Germany.
readings.contentNote: Barbara compares the old man to “a heathen or an old Indian,” a dated and insulting comparison that shows the villagers’ fear and prejudice rather than the author’s judgment of the grandfather.

excerpt.locator: Chapter I, “Going Up to the Alm-Uncle,” from the opening to Barbara’s promise to keep a secret; opens “The little old town of Mayenfeld is charmingly situated. From it a footpath leads through…”; closes “…keep things to myself, if I have to. You won't repent of having told me, I assure you!"”.

questions.prompt: Why is Heidi so hot on a sunny June morning?
facilitatorNotes: She is wearing two or three dresses, a large red shawl and heavy hob-nailed boots, “as if she had to brave a bitter frost.” The narrator’s “Small wonder though!” asks readers to notice. Readers will learn the reason for the layers later in the chapter.
evidence: bundled up as if she had to brave a bitter frost
she wore two dresses, if not three

questions.prompt: What does Barbara believe about the Alm-Uncle, and where have her ideas come from?
facilitatorNotes: She says he speaks to no one, stays away from church and frightens everyone with his eyebrows and beard. But she has lived in the village only since her marriage, and people speak of him “as if they were afraid.” Her picture is built from rumour, not from knowing him.
evidence: We all fear him
Nobody had a good word for him

questions.prompt: Deta says, “He won't do her any harm; and if he should, he is responsible, not I.” What does this show about her?
facilitatorNotes: She has decided to take her new job and wants to be free of blame in advance, even though she is not sure the plan is safe. Some readers will add that she has cared for Heidi for four years and needs to earn a living; both views can use the text.
evidence: if he should, he is responsible, not I
The child shall not hinder me from accepting it, I tell you that!

questions.prompt: Barbara says, “People do not gossip much in Praetiggan.” Why might a reader smile at that?
facilitatorNotes: She has “long been anxious” to hear about the old man and grabs Deta’s arm to get the secret, so she is gossiping while she denies it. The gap between what she says and what she does is gentle comedy.
evidence: People do not gossip much in Praetiggan
Barbara had long been anxious to know something about the old uncle

readings.title: Heidi: the Alm-Uncle’s story (Chapter I, second part)
readings.challenge: Keep track of a family history told in one long speech, and remember who is telling it.
readings.focus: Deta’s story explains the old man’s loneliness, but she has her own reasons for telling it this way.
readings.context: Recap: Deta is taking Heidi up the mountain to leave her with her grandfather, the Alm-Uncle, whom the villagers fear. Barbara, a neighbour, has begged to hear his story. A goatherd looks after goats on the pasture; an apprentice who finishes training becomes a master of his trade.
readings.contentNote: Deta tells how Heidi’s father was killed by a falling beam and her mother died soon after of grief and fever. She also says the grandfather lost his farm through drinking and gambling.

excerpt.locator: Chapter I, “Going Up to the Alm-Uncle,” from Deta’s search for Heidi through the description of Peter’s family; opens “"All right, but keep your word!" said Deta warningly. Then she looked around to see that…”; closes “…blind grandmother was called by young and old from many miles about just "grandmother."”.

questions.prompt: Where is Heidi while the two women talk, and how does Deta react when she sees her?
facilitatorNotes: Heidi has gone off with Peter and the goats, and the women “had not noticed her absence” for some time. Deta is glad Peter can watch her so the story can go on without interruption. Readers may see this as carelessness, or as trust in a child who “keeps her eyes wide open.”
evidence: they had not noticed her absence
she is bright for her five years and keeps her eyes wide open

questions.prompt: List the losses in the old man’s life. Which one does Deta say changed him most?
facilitatorNotes: He lost his farm “with drink and play,” his parents died of grief, his son Tobias was killed, and Tobias’s wife Adelheid died. Deta says that after his son’s death he never spoke to anyone again.
evidence: he soon lost everything with drink and play
After the death of his son he never spoke to a living soul.

questions.prompt: “People said that heaven had punished the uncle for his misdeeds.” Is Deta telling what is true, or what people say? Why does it matter?
facilitatorNotes: She repeats the village’s judgment and admits “many strange rumors” went round. She cannot prove them, and she wants to justify leaving Heidi with him, so readers should hold her account at a distance.
evidence: People said that heaven had punished the uncle for his misdeeds.
Many strange rumors went round about the uncle

questions.prompt: What do we learn about Peter’s life from the last long paragraph?
facilitatorNotes: He spends every day alone with the goats, sees other children only in the evening, and lives with his mother and his blind grandmother; his father died in an accident. The paragraph prepares for the friendships Heidi will make.
evidence: the rest of the day the animals were his sole companions
At home lived his mother and an old blind grandmother

readings.title: Heidi: a heap of clothes on the hillside (Chapter I, third part)
readings.challenge: Compare how two characters judge the same action.
readings.focus: Heidi solves her own problem in a way that shocks her aunt.
readings.context: Recap: Deta has told Barbara the sad story of Heidi’s family and of the grandfather, who turned away from everyone after his son died. Meanwhile Heidi has been climbing behind Peter the goatherd. A petticoat is a light underskirt; a five-penny-piece is a small coin.

excerpt.locator: Chapter I, “Going Up to the Alm-Uncle,” from Deta’s wait above Peter’s hut until Peter carries the bundle; opens “Deta waited about ten minutes to see if the children were coming up behind with the…”; closes “…and his right swinging the stick. Heidi jumped along gaily by his side with the goats.”.

questions.prompt: Why does Heidi take off her clothes? What explanation does the narrator give?
facilitatorNotes: She is panting in heavy clothes and envies Peter’s bare feet and the goats’ slender legs. The narrator explains that Deta had dressed her in her Sunday clothes over her workday ones to avoid carrying them. Heidi’s choice is practical.
evidence: To save the trouble of carrying them, her aunt had dressed her in her Sunday clothes over her workday garments.
She was now as light-footed as any of them.

questions.prompt: Deta calls Heidi stupid; Heidi says, “Because I do not need them.” Who do you think is right?
facilitatorNotes: Deta worries about the new shoes and the stockings she made herself; Heidi thinks only of comfort and is not sorry. Notice that Heidi folded her dresses neatly. Each has a reason, and readers may side with either.
evidence: Because I do not need them
Heidi arranged her dresses neatly in a heap

questions.prompt: What do Peter’s grin, his silence and the coin tell you about him?
facilitatorNotes: He grins wider and wider but says nothing; he will not move until Deta offers money, then runs fast. The coin is “a treasure” he seldom gets, which hints at how poor his family is.
evidence: he grinned yet more, till his mouth seemed to reach from ear to ear; but he said never a word
He did not often get such a treasure

readings.title: Heidi: “Good evening, grandfather!” (Chapter I, end)
readings.challenge: Read faces, gestures and silences as carefully as words.
readings.focus: The meeting everyone feared takes a few lines; Deta’s uneasy conscience sends her running.
readings.context: Recap: Heidi has shed her heavy clothes and climbed with Peter and the goats, and Deta paid Peter to fetch the bundle. Now they reach the grandfather’s hut at the top. A conscience is the inner sense of right and wrong.

excerpt.locator: Chapter I, “Going Up to the Alm-Uncle,” from the grandfather’s hut to the end of the chapter; opens “After three quarters of an hour they reached the height where the hut of the old man…”; closes “…who interfered in her affairs, and looked forward with great delight to her new place.”.

questions.prompt: How does Heidi greet her grandfather, and how is this different from what the villagers would expect?
facilitatorNotes: She reaches him first, holds out her hand and says good evening, then studies him “with much curiosity.” The villagers fear him; Heidi looks back at him without fear.
evidence: Heidi reached the top first
Heidi gazed back at him with an unwinking glance and examined him with much curiosity

questions.prompt: Deta “had said more in her excitement than she had intended.” What did she say, and why does it anger the old man?
facilitatorNotes: She tells him that if Heidi comes to harm he is responsible and that he would not want to “burden your conscience any further,” which reminds him of his past. The narrator adds that her own conscience was “not quite clear.”
evidence: I am sure you do not want to burden your conscience any further
just because her conscience was not quite clear

questions.prompt: Why is Deta uneasy as she runs down the mountain, and how does she comfort herself?
facilitatorNotes: The village women cry “The poor little dear!”, and she remembers her mother asked her on her deathbed to care for Heidi. She tells herself she can help more by earning money. Readers can decide whether that is a reason or an excuse.
evidence: to tell the truth, she herself was uneasy
she would be able to do more for the child if she could earn some money

questions.prompt: Are there any clues that the grandfather may not be as terrible as people say?
facilitatorNotes: He sits quietly watching the children climb, and his first worry is being “helpless” if she cries, not that she will be a nuisance. His anger is aimed at Deta, not Heidi. Other readers may think the clues are too few to judge yet.
evidence: He quietly watched the children climbing up with the goats
then I'll be helpless

readings.title: Heidi: the pastor’s visit (Chapter V, first part)
readings.challenge: Weigh two adults’ arguments about what is best for a child.
readings.focus: The grandfather wants Heidi “free and happy as a bird”; the pastor says she must learn.
readings.context: Heidi (1880–81) is by the Swiss writer Johanna Spyri; this English translation by Elisabeth P. Stork appeared in 1915. Earlier chapters: Heidi, an orphan, was left by her aunt Deta with her grandfather, the Alm-Uncle, who lives alone high on a Swiss mountain pasture and avoids the village. Heidi has come to love him, the goats, Peter the goatherd and Peter’s blind grandmother, whose cottage the grandfather has mended. A parson or pastor is the minister of the village church.

excerpt.locator: Chapter V, “Two Visitors,” from the opening through the pastor’s departure; opens “Two winters had nearly passed. Heidi was happy, for the spring was coming again, with the…”; closes “"God be with you," said the parson, and left him sadly.”.

questions.prompt: What reasons does the grandfather give for keeping Heidi out of school? Which seems strongest to you?
facilitatorNotes: He wants her free; the walk is two hours through wind and storm; and her mother was delicate, with sleep-walking and fainting fits. The pastor himself agrees that the walk is too much.
evidence: I want her to be free and happy as a bird!
It is a two hours' walk, and I shall not let her go

questions.prompt: Which part of the old man’s argument does the pastor accept, and what does he suggest instead?
facilitatorNotes: He agrees she cannot go to school from the mountain, and suggests the grandfather come back to live in the village and make his peace.
evidence: You could not send her to school from here.
Why don't you come down to live among us again?

questions.prompt: “The people there and I despise each other.” Does the pastor’s visit show that the village feels that way about the grandfather?
facilitatorNotes: The pastor calls him “neighbor,” shakes his hand and promises a glad welcome, so at least one villager does not despise him. The old man may be wrong about the village, or the pastor may speak only for himself.
evidence: the people there and I despise each other
We shall receive you gladly, reconciled with God and man.

readings.title: Heidi: Aunt Deta comes back (Chapter V, end)
readings.challenge: Notice when a character tells only part of the truth to get what she wants.
readings.focus: Deta talks Heidi away from the mountain with promises she does not mean.
readings.context: Recap: the village pastor has climbed up to tell the grandfather that Heidi, now nearly eight, must go to school, and has urged him to move back to the village. The old man refused. Deta now works for a rich family in Frankfurt. A dress with a train has a long back that sweeps along the floor.

excerpt.locator: Chapter V, “Two Visitors,” from Deta’s arrival to the end of the chapter; opens “The old man was out of humor that day, and when Heidi begged to go to the grandmother, he…”; closes “…could hear Heidi's voice before I die," the poor old woman would exclaim, day after day.”.

questions.prompt: Which words does Deta use to make the place in Frankfurt sound wonderful?
facilitatorNotes: “A splendid chance,” the “largest house in Frankfurt,” “very rich relations,” and “a lucky chance.” The child there is a lame girl who needs a companion for her lessons.
evidence: she had found a splendid chance for her
who owned the largest house in Frankfurt

questions.prompt: What does Deta threaten when the grandfather refuses, and why might he give in?
facilitatorNotes: She says she will get people to back her and that in court old stories “might be warmed up.” He storms out with “Take her and ruin her.” Readers may see hurt pride and anger, or a fear of his past being told; both fit.
evidence: some things might be warmed up that you would not care to hear about
Take her and ruin her

questions.prompt: Heidi asks, “Can I come home again to-night?” Is Deta’s answer honest?
facilitatorNotes: She never says yes to tonight; she says “I told you you could come back” and talks of trains that “fly.” She also uses Heidi’s wish to bring rolls to the grandmother to hurry her along. She is leading Heidi on.
evidence: Come now, I told you you could come back.
She also suggested that Heidi might bring a lovely present to the grandmother when she came back.

questions.prompt: The villagers decide Heidi was glad to go. Why are they wrong, and who alone speaks up for the grandfather?
facilitatorNotes: They saw her hurrying, but she hurried so she could return sooner with the rolls. Only Peter’s blind grandmother tells of the old man’s care, and people “only half believed” her.
evidence: they thought that she had been glad to go
The old grandmother alone stuck to him faithfully.

readings.title: Heidi: arriving at the Sesemann house (Chapter VI, opening)
readings.challenge: Hear how a new place is shown through the way people speak.
readings.focus: A grand house full of servants and rules meets a child who answers every question honestly.
readings.context: Recap: Aunt Deta has taken Heidi from her grandfather to Frankfurt, promising she can soon go home with soft white rolls for Peter’s grandmother. Now they arrive at the house of Mr. Sesemann, whose daughter Clara cannot walk. A butler and a maid are servants; a housekeeper runs a household. A Christian name is the first name given at baptism.
readings.contentNote: Deta gives Heidi two small blows to stop her answering, and the housekeeper calls her ignorant.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VI, “A New Chapter with New Things,” from the opening until Deta hurries away; opens “In a beautiful house in Frankfurt lived a sick child by the name of Clara Sesemann. She…”; closes “…her and tried to call her back, for she wanted to ask Deta a number of questions.”.

questions.prompt: The coachman and the butler both say, “That's not my business.” What does the repeated line suggest about this house?
facilitatorNotes: Each servant has one job and passes Deta on to the next, and the maid speaks “scornfully.” The house is grand, formal and not very welcoming.
evidence: That's not my business
asked scornfully

questions.prompt: Why does Deta say Heidi is “about ten,” and how does Heidi spoil the story?
facilitatorNotes: The family wanted a companion of twelve to share Clara’s lessons, so Deta makes Heidi older. Heidi repeats what her grandfather told her: she is eight.
evidence: I think she is about ten years old.
Grandfather said that I was eight years old

questions.prompt: Heidi answers “None” and “Nothing.” Is she being pert, as Miss Rottenmeier wonders, or honest?
facilitatorNotes: The narrator says she replied “truthfully” and did not even know why she was being hit. Readers may feel Miss Rottenmeier judges her by city expectations; others may understand the housekeeper’s surprise.
evidence: replied Heidi, truthfully
as the child had no idea why, she did not get embarrassed

readings.title: Heidi: a turtle and a basket of kittens (Chapter VIII, first part)
readings.challenge: Enjoy a comic scene, and notice how each character reacts to the same surprise.
readings.focus: A street-boy with a barrel-organ and a basket of kittens turn the morning lessons upside down.
readings.context: Heidi (1880–81) is by the Swiss writer Johanna Spyri; this English translation by Elisabeth P. Stork appeared in 1915. Eight-year-old Heidi has been taken from her grandfather’s hut on a Swiss mountain to Frankfurt, a big city in Germany, to keep company with Clara Sesemann, a rich girl who cannot walk and is pushed about in a rolling-chair. Miss Rottenmeier is the strict housekeeper, Sebastian the butler and Tinette a maid; Clara calls her tutor “Mr. Candidate.” Miss Rottenmeier insists on Heidi’s full name, Adelheid. The day before, Heidi slipped out to look for the mountains from a church tower. A street-boy showed her the way, and she promised him money that Clara would pay; the old tower-keeper offered her as many kittens as she had room for. A barrel-organ plays tunes when its handle is turned; an urchin is a ragged child; “cunning” here means sweet and lively.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VIII, “Great Disturbances in the Sesemann House,” from the opening until Clara asks Miss Rottenmeier to wait for her father; opens “A short time after the tutor had arrived next morning, the door-bell rang so violently…”; closes “…and the lady often felt discouraged, though nothing remarkable happened for a few days.”.

questions.prompt: How does the street-boy convince Sebastian that he has met someone from this house? Why does Sebastian chuckle?
facilitatorNotes: He describes curly hair, black eyes and a funny way of talking. Sebastian knows Clara never goes out, so he realizes the boy means Heidi, “the little Miss,” and guesses there will be fun.
evidence: She has curly hair, black eyes and talks in a funny way.
"Oh," Sebastian chuckled to himself, "that was the little Miss."

questions.prompt: Sebastian “had seen everything behind the door.” Whose side is he on, and how can you tell?
facilitatorNotes: He lets the boy in, enjoys the “great scene,” and pays him forty pennies from Clara and forty more for playing. He seems to enjoy Miss Rottenmeier’s fright and to like the children. Readers might also say he is simply kind to a poor boy.
evidence: for he had seen everything behind the door, and a great scene it had been!
It was well done, my boy.

questions.prompt: Find two signs that Clara enjoys the disturbances. Why might a day like this matter so much to her?
facilitatorNotes: She is delighted by the interruption, begs to peep into the basket and calls out at the kittens. She cannot walk and her lessons are dull, so a morning with no time for yawning is a treat.
evidence: Clara, delighted at his interruption
No time had been found for yawning that day, either!

questions.prompt: Why doesn’t the cellar frighten Heidi? Why might Clara ask Miss Rottenmeier to wait for Papa?
facilitatorNotes: Her grandfather’s cellar held milk and cheese and no rats. Clara may hope her father will be gentler, or she may just want to save her friend; readers can decide.
evidence: A cellar held no terrors for Heidi
you must wait till Papa comes home, and then he can punish Heidi

readings.title: Heidi: the bread in the wardrobe (Chapter VIII, end)
readings.challenge: Follow a character’s feelings when the grown-ups around her cannot understand them.
readings.focus: Heidi tries to go home, is scolded, and loses the rolls she has saved for the grandmother.
readings.context: Recap: a street-boy’s barrel-organ, a turtle and a basket of kittens have turned the Sesemann house upside down, and Miss Rottenmeier wanted to shut Heidi in the cellar until Clara asked her to wait for Mr. Sesemann, Clara’s father. On the mountain Heidi often visited the blind grandmother of Peter the goatherd. The black bread there is too hard for the old woman, so Heidi has been saving soft white rolls to take her. Snowhopper and Thistlefinch are goats in Peter’s herd. Heidi’s aunt, who brought her to Frankfurt, told her she could go back if she wished. A vagabond is a homeless wanderer; a wardrobe is a cupboard for clothes.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VIII, “Great Disturbances in the Sesemann House,” from Heidi’s evenings with Clara to the end of the chapter; opens “Clara, on the contrary, enjoyed her companion's society, for she always did funny things.…”; closes “…and wrapping it in a handkerchief, she hid it in the furthest corner of her wardrobe.”.

questions.prompt: What does Heidi take when she sets off for home? What do her choices tell you?
facilitatorNotes: Only the bread, wrapped in her red shawl, and her old straw hat. She means to keep her promise to the grandmother; she wants nothing from the rich house.
evidence: In a great hurry she packed the bread in the red shawl, and putting on her old straw hat, started off.

questions.prompt: Miss Rottenmeier asks about food, service and a fine room; Heidi answers with Snowhopper, the grandmother and the sunset. Why do they seem to be talking about different things?
facilitatorNotes: Miss Rottenmeier thinks a child should be grateful for comfort and money; Heidi is longing for the creatures and people she loves and for the mountains. Miss Rottenmeier hears only nonsense and calls her crazy; the reader hears homesickness.
evidence: Have you ever before had such food, service and such a room?
I must see the sun again when he says good-night to the mountains
For mercy's sake, the child is crazy!

questions.prompt: How does Sebastian help Heidi? Find two things he says or does.
facilitatorNotes: He cheers her on the stairs and promises to show her the kittens; later he rescues her straw hat and hides it in her bed, after trying to signal to her at supper.
evidence: Don't give in! Don't be so sad!
So Sebastian had saved it for her and had tried to tell her!

questions.prompt: Clara says the stale rolls “were not fit to eat.” Is she right? Why do they matter so much to Heidi?
facilitatorNotes: Clara is practical and kind, and promises fresher rolls. For Heidi the rolls are a promise to the blind grandmother and a link with home, so losing them hurts more than losing bread. Both girls are right in their own way.
evidence: Those were not fit to eat, Heidi.
Oh, they were for grandmother!

readings.title: Heidi: Mr. Sesemann comes home (Chapter IX)
readings.challenge: Compare what different people say about the same child, and decide whom to believe.
readings.focus: Clara’s father hears Miss Rottenmeier’s complaints and makes up his own mind about Heidi.
readings.context: Recap: Heidi’s first weeks in Frankfurt have been full of trouble. A barrel-organ, a turtle and a basket of kittens upset the lessons; when Heidi tried to go home, Miss Rottenmeier called her ungrateful and thought her mind was wrong; and the rolls Heidi had saved for the blind grandmother on the mountain were thrown away. Mr. Sesemann, Clara’s father, is often away on business in Paris. Long-winded means talking far too long; a pendant hangs from a chain; peculiarities are odd habits.

excerpt.locator: Chapter IX, “The Master of the House Hears of Strange Doings,” the whole chapter; opens “A few days afterwards there was great excitement in the Sesemann residence, for the…”; closes “…Rottenmeier's disapproval, who thought that the child was not entitled to this intimacy.”.

questions.prompt: Miss Rottenmeier hoped Heidi would go through life “hardly touching the earth.” How does Mr. Sesemann answer, and what does his joke show about him?
facilitatorNotes: He says even Swiss children are made to touch the earth, or they would need wings. He gently mocks her fancy idea; he is good-humoured and sensible.
evidence: hardly touching the earth
otherwise they would have to have wings

questions.prompt: Mr. Sesemann asks the tutor and then Clara about Heidi. Why does he learn more from Clara?
facilitatorNotes: The tutor talks at great length without answering; Clara tells what actually happened and explains Heidi’s speeches, and her father laughs. A child who lives with Heidi turns out to be the best witness.
evidence: had to listen to very long-winded explanations of the child's character
Clara now began to relate to her father all the incidents with the kittens and the turtle

questions.prompt: Why does Mr. Sesemann send Heidi for a glass of water? What does she do, and what does it show about her?
facilitatorNotes: He wants her out of the room so he can ask Clara privately. Heidi takes him at his word and walks past two crowded fountains to a third, where she meets a gentleman. It shows how independent and determined she is, and how little she knows of city ways; readers may think it brave or risky.
evidence: get me--get me a glass of water
I had to go down another street and there I got it.

questions.prompt: Mr. Sesemann orders that Heidi’s “peculiarities must not be punished.” Will things be better for Heidi now? What clues point each way?
facilitatorNotes: He is on her side and his mother is coming to help. But he stays only two weeks, Miss Rottenmeier is not pleased, and nobody has noticed how homesick Heidi is. Readers can argue either way.
evidence: Her peculiarities must not be punished.
but she was not very much pleased at the prospect

readings.title: Heidi: the book and the forbidden tears (Chapter XI)
readings.challenge: Use a chapter title to weigh what a character gains against what she loses.
readings.focus: Heidi learns to read and sew, but grows sadder and more silent.
readings.context: Heidi (1880–81) is by the Swiss writer Johanna Spyri; this English translation by Elisabeth P. Stork appeared in 1915. Heidi has been taken from her grandfather’s hut in the Swiss Alps to Frankfurt, a city in Germany, as a companion for Clara Sesemann, who cannot walk. Clara’s kind grandmother, Mrs. Sesemann, has come to stay. She gave Heidi a book of pictures and stories, helped her learn to read at last, and told her she could tell her sorrow to God, so Heidi prayed to go home. The grandmother Heidi weeps for here is a different one: the blind grandmother of Peter the goatherd, whom Heidi visited on the mountain and promised to bring soft rolls. Miss Rottenmeier is the strict housekeeper; Adelheid is Heidi’s full name. To confide is to tell someone a secret; an affliction is a suffering.
readings.contentNote: The chapter is about Christian prayer, and the story treats Mrs. Sesemann’s teaching as true. Heidi weeps over a story of a grandmother’s death, and grows thin and pale with homesickness.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XI, “Heidi Gains in Some Respects and Loses in Others,” the whole chapter; opens “The grandmama sent for Heidi every day after dinner, while Clara was resting and Miss…”; closes “…would remain, eating her heart away with longing, till Clara would call for her to come.”.

questions.prompt: What does Heidi gain in this chapter, and what does she lose?
facilitatorNotes: She gains sewing, reading and the stories, and the comfort of trusting in God again. She loses her cheerfulness, her appetite, her health and even the freedom to cry.
evidence: Unconsciously Heidi had learned to sew
her eyes never sparkled merrily as before

questions.prompt: Why has Heidi stopped praying, and how does Mrs. Sesemann answer her?
facilitatorNotes: Heidi thinks God cannot hear everyone in Frankfurt and has not granted her wish. Mrs. Sesemann says God knows better than we do what we need and will answer in time. Students may hold different beliefs; keep the talk on each character’s reasons and on how the answer changes Heidi.
evidence: if all the people in Frankfurt pray every night, He cannot listen to them all
He gives us something much better

questions.prompt: Why does a story about a grandmother’s death upset Heidi so much?
facilitatorNotes: Whatever she reads seems real to her, so she believes Peter’s grandmother has died without ever getting a roll, and she fears her grandfather may die while she is far away.
evidence: Whatever Heidi read always seemed real to her
and she never got one single roll!

questions.prompt: After Miss Rottenmeier’s threat, “Heidi never cried again.” Did the threat solve anything? What does the last paragraph show?
facilitatorNotes: It only hid the sadness. Heidi makes strange faces to hold back sobs, cries quietly at night, stops eating and covers her eyes against the sunshine on the wall. Most readers will see that the threat made things worse.
evidence: After that Heidi never cried again
eating her heart away with longing

readings.title: Heidi: a ghost in the house (Chapter XII, first part)
readings.challenge: Sort a mystery’s facts from the guesses people make about them.
readings.focus: Every morning the front door is found open, and the household believes a ghost is walking.
readings.context: Recap: Clara’s grandmother has gone home. Heidi, forbidden by Miss Rottenmeier to cry, has grown thin, pale and silent with longing for her grandfather and the mountains. Mr. Sesemann, Clara’s father, is away on business in Paris. John is another of the servants; Tinette is a maid. Liquor is strong drink; to despatch something is to get rid of it quickly; a person’s constitution is their general health; venerable ancestors are respected forefathers; expiating means making up for a wrong. Dr. Classen is the old doctor Heidi met at the fountain.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XII, “The Sesemann House Is Haunted,” from the opening until Mr. Sesemann explains his suspicions to the doctor; opens “For several days Miss Rottenmeier had been wandering silently about the house. When she…”; closes “…of thieves, who, after intimidating the people, would surely rob his house by and by.”.

questions.prompt: What are the facts of the mystery? List what the servants find every morning and what John says he saw.
facilitatorNotes: The front door is wide open even with double locks, yet nothing is missing; John says he saw a white form go up the stairs. Everything else is fear and guessing.
evidence: they found the front door wide open
but nothing was missing
a white form was on the stairs

questions.prompt: How does the fear spread through the house? Find two people it reaches.
facilitatorNotes: Miss Rottenmeier glances behind her and takes Tinette everywhere; the servants go in pairs; the cook mutters; Sebastian shivers though he saw nothing; Clara will not stay alone. The story frightens people more than anything they have seen.
evidence: none of the servants dared to go anywhere alone
Clara, at the uncanny tale, immediately exclaimed that she would not stay alone another moment

questions.prompt: Why does Mr. Sesemann ignore the first letter but come home after the second?
facilitatorNotes: The first is all about Miss Rottenmeier’s own fright, so he jokes and suggests his mother. The second warns that the fright could harm Clara’s health, and he comes for his daughter’s sake. Readers may notice that Miss Rottenmeier learns how to get her way.
evidence: Miss Rottenmeier was offended with the tone of the letter
the excitement might have serious effects on his daughter's delicate constitution

questions.prompt: Heidi “did not know what ghosts were” and stays calm. Why might the author mention her just here?
facilitatorNotes: It sets her apart from the frightened household, and an alert reader may wonder about the one person nobody suspects. Others may take it simply as a sign of her innocence. Either reading is fair before the ending.
evidence: while Heidi, who did not know what ghosts were, was perfectly unmoved

readings.title: Heidi: the doctor’s prescription (Chapter XII, end)
readings.challenge: Notice how a doctor’s questions uncover the truth, and judge what he decides.
readings.focus: The ghost is caught, and the doctor finds out what is really wrong with Heidi.
readings.context: Recap: every morning the Sesemanns’ front door has been found open, and the servants believe a white ghost walks at night. Mr. Sesemann has come home from Paris and asked his old friend Dr. Classen to sit up with him to catch it. A candelabrum (plural candelabra) holds several candles. A sleep-walker gets up and moves about while still asleep. A prescription is a doctor’s order for treatment; bracing mountain air is fresh and strengthening. “Threshhold” is how this printing spells threshold.
readings.contentNote: The two men carry loaded revolvers to meet the “ghost.” The doctor finds Heidi so homesick that she has become ill.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XII, “The Sesemann House Is Haunted,” from the night watch to the end of the chapter; opens “With these explanations they entered the room where the two servants had watched before.…”; closes “…his leave, for the morning had already come and the sun was shining in through the door.”.

questions.prompt: How does the author build suspense before the ghost appears?
facilitatorNotes: The men wait until one o’clock in total quiet; the doctor raises a finger; the bar, the key and the door move one after another; then a still white form stands in the moonlight.
evidence: Suddenly the doctor raised his finger.
the bar was unfastened, the key was turned, and the door flew open

questions.prompt: Which of the doctor’s questions finally makes Heidi cry, and why that one?
facilitatorNotes: “But wasn't it a little lonely there?” She answers that it was beautiful and then breaks down: the memory of home, the fright of the night and all her held-back sorrow come out together.
evidence: "But wasn't it a little lonely there?"
all the restrained sorrow overpowered the child

questions.prompt: Heidi says “Oh yes” when asked whether she likes it in Frankfurt. Is she telling the truth? Why might she answer that way?
facilitatorNotes: Her “faint, uncertain” voice says no. She has been called ungrateful and forbidden to cry, so she has learned to hide her feelings. Some readers may think she also does not want to hurt Clara.
evidence: "Oh yes," was the faint, uncertain reply.
Oh no, I must never do that, for Miss Rottenmeier has forbidden it.

questions.prompt: Why does Mr. Sesemann refuse at first to send Heidi home, and what changes his mind?
facilitatorNotes: He is ashamed to send back a sick child who came to him healthy and wants her cured first. The doctor says no medicine can cure homesickness and that she may never get well in the city. Readers may discuss whether he cares more about Heidi or about how it looks.
evidence: when she has come in good health?
We cannot cure her with powders and pills.
